 Microsoft buys $1 billion of non-voting Anthropic stock in the IPO
 Microsoft will buy about $1 billion of non-voting Class N shares in Anthropic's IPO private placement. That is 0.1% of the company, not an acquisition.

 Microsoft is not buying Anthropic. In the Nasdaq listing prospectus filed on November 10, 2026, the Redmond giant is in fact one of the seven buyers of non-voting Class N shares that Anthropic will sell in a $26 billion private placement. Its slice is worth about $1 billion , or 0.1% of the shares outstanding after the deal.
 Anthropic is the San Francisco company that develops Claude and that on October 26 applied to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT (the roadshow , the tour of investor presentations, kicked off on November 10). A private placement is a sale of shares to a handful of chosen investors, outside the stock exchange. It runs in parallel with the public offering open to everyone, the IPO (initial public offering, the first sale of shares to the public).
 Signing on alongside Microsoft are Google and Nvidia at $10 billion each, AMD at $2.5 billion, Broadcom and Micron at $1 billion apiece, and TSMC Partners at $500 million. Google sells cloud and is among Anthropic's longtime shareholders. Nvidia makes the graphics cards (GPUs) that a large share of artificial intelligence models run on, AMD is its direct rival, Broadcom designs custom chips, Micron makes memory, and TSMC Partners belongs to the Taiwanese TSMC group, the foundry that prints the chips for half the sector.
 The seven buyers of Anthropic Class N shares and the amounts expected under the prospectus 
 How much is Microsoft's stake in Anthropic worth?
 Microsoft's stake is worth about $1 billion, equal to 13,513,513 Class N shares if the IPO prices at $74, the midpoint of the $70 to $78 range given in Anthropic's roadshow announcement . Out of the 13.09 billion shares expected after the deal, all classes included, that comes to 0.1%. The math is ours, based on the figures in the second amendment to the prospectus (S-1/A) .
 The commitment is expressed in dollars, not shares, so the share count moves with the final price. At $70 Microsoft would receive about 14.3 million, at $78 about 12.8 million, still for $1 billion. The whole placement, at $74, comes to 351,351,348 shares, or 2.7% of the total.
 Buyer 
 Expected amount 
 What it already gives Anthropic 
 Google $10 billion Cloud and capital 
 Nvidia $10 billion Graphics cards (GPUs) 
 AMD $2.5 billion Processors and accelerators 
 Broadcom $1 billion Custom chips 
 Micron $1 billion Memory 
 Microsoft $1 billion Azure cloud 
 TSMC Partners $500 million Chip manufacturing 
 Google and Nvidia alone account for 77% of the $26 billion. For Mountain View, though, it isn't fresh money. The prospectus explains that the purchase serves to fund part of the investments the group had already promised Anthropic under a 2026 agreement, so the placement is also a way to tidy up existing commitments.
 Non-voting shares, so no control
 Class N shares carry no voting rights on any matter, except where required by law (for example, certain charter amendments that would worsen the rights of that class alone). They can be converted into Class A shares, the same ones that will list on the Nasdaq. Buyers, then, share in profits and any appreciation, but count for nothing at the shareholder meeting.
 Control sits elsewhere. A single Class F share, held by Founder LLC (the entity of the seven cofounders), will carry 50.1% of the votes on general matters, including the election of directors (except those of Class T). It carries no economic rights. That percentage stays fixed even when Anthropic issues new shares. When all is said and done, not even someone who bought up the entire listed portion could exceed 49.9% of the votes. A takeover is de facto off the table.
 The real tie is the cloud
 At Redmond the billion in shares matters less than the contract that comes with it. In November 2025 Microsoft and Nvidia announced a deal with Anthropic, with up to $5 billion from Microsoft, up to $10 billion from Nvidia and $30 billion of Azure capacity that Anthropic committed to buy. That agreement was reworked between February and November 2026. Today the prospectus sets the bar higher.
 Anthropic has in fact committed to spend at least $47.2 billion with Microsoft, up to a maximum of $49.2 billion, between November 2026 and June 2033, regardless of actual usage. The commitment can't be canceled, except for a serious uncured breach by Microsoft or, tranche by tranche, for missed deliveries. A billion in shares against at least $47.2 billion of guaranteed spend works out to a ratio of about 47 to 1 (the calculation is ours).
 To gauge the weight of the contract, look at the other two big clouds. With Google the minimum commitment is about $121.3 billion between April 2026 and July 2033, with Amazon at least $110 billion between May 2026 and April 2036. In both cases, if actual spend stays under the threshold, Anthropic has to pay the difference. Microsoft, in essence, is the smallest of the three cloud providers (our comparison, based on the prospectus figures).
 The same pattern applies to the other six, who are already suppliers of chips, memory or computing capacity, as investingLive points out in the wake of a document seen by Reuters. To critics the money flows back home. It is so-called circular financing, a theme Trending Topics picks up from Reuters in connection with this deal.
 What can still change
 The prospectus is not yet effective, so no shares can be sold or bought. Final pricing is expected for Wednesday, November 18, with the debut on Thursday, November 19, according to the financial press, while Anthropic has not confirmed the dates. The private placement, for its part, closes right after the IPO and requires shareholder approval, which the company says it expects before closing. The IPO, by contrast, does not depend on the placement.
 Estimates of the company's value also remain, and they diverge. Renaissance Capital calculates $1.2 trillion at the midpoint of the range (not counting $111 billion of convertible debt), while the figures attributed to CNBC run from about $1.26 trillion to $1.4 trillion. A week ago, after all, investors had balked at $1.5 trillion . The November 10 document comes eight days after the first amendment , the one that had sparked debate over the AI acceleration threshold.
 Microsoft between OpenAI and Anthropic
 Microsoft is no newcomer, either. In the quarter ended in June it booked a $3.2 billion gain on its Anthropic stake . It also keeps its OpenAI stake in the portfolio. The prospectus, for its part, warns that Amazon, Google and Microsoft are at once suppliers, customers, financiers and competitors of Anthropic, each with its own models.
 It shows inside the company too. In June the Redmond giant had blocked Claude Fable 5 for its employees over a data retention issue, while with Google it takes on Anthropic and OpenAI on coding models . Ally and rival, in effect, in the same stock-market filing.
 Frequently asked questions
 1. Can I buy the shares Microsoft and the others are buying?
 No, because the Class N shares in the private placement are reserved for the seven investors who signed and can't be bought on the stock exchange. The public will be able to aim at the IPO, which covers Class A shares, with rules that differ from country to country (here we explained who can buy them and why Italy is left out ).
 2. How much does Anthropic take in between the IPO and the placement?
 Anthropic takes in about $84.6 billion net at a price of $74, or about $93.7 billion if the underwriters exercise the option for additional shares, the prospectus estimates. It will pay no fees on the private placement, so the full $26 billion goes straight into the company's coffers.
 3. Can Microsoft resell the Class N shares right away?
 Microsoft can't freely resell them on the stock exchange. The shares are not registered, so they can only be resold with an effective registration or under an exemption such as Rule 144 (the US rule on unregistered securities), and some buyers have registration rights. Unlike the shares of employees and directors, though, they are not subject to the lock-ups agreed with the underwriters.
 4. What happens if the IPO doesn't close?
 The private placement falls through with it. The prospectus makes it conditional on completion of the IPO, in addition to shareholder approval, while the IPO can close without the placement.
 The weight of a billion
 For Microsoft the billion in non-voting shares weighs little but binds a lot. Anthropic remains a customer worth at least $47.2 billion of spend through 2033. If the market rewards the IPO, the stake Redmond already holds in its portfolio gains value along with the new one. For Anthropic the opposite holds, because a company with three clouds among its shareholders still depends (and heavily) on whoever rents it the chips. A marriage of convenience, the non-voting kind.
